# Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation Errors Matter in AI-Driven Systems Research?

Jinwoo Hwang    Sukmin Cho    Tao Zhang Affiliation: Microsoft Research
Asia    Soheil Abbasloo   Jongse Park   Peng Cheng
Affiliation: Microsoft Research Asia Affiliation: KAIST

###### Abstract

LLM agents increasingly drive systems research and rely on simulators to
evaluate candidate designs at scale. Simulators are imperfect by design:
their modeling limitations can distort predictions yet leave the
recommended design correct, or change which design should be selected.
We introduce Siris to test whether LLMs can tell these cases apart,
judging from their systems understanding when a limitation invalidates
the simulator’s recommendation. By perturbing a simulator, Siris
constructs workload pairs with the same candidates, limitation, and
simulator recommendation. The perturbation changes predictions on both
workloads, yet a reference simulator supports the recommendation on only
one. Evaluating thirteen frontier LLMs on LLM serving design problems,
we find that identifying a limitation does not ensure a correct choice,
and even the strongest models sometimes abandon valid recommendations.
Self-correction through a review turn helps these models restore valid
choices but introduces new errors in several others. These findings
motivate evaluating systems understanding through design decisions under
imperfect simulators.

Research Asia.  
^(†)Corresponding author.

## 1 Introduction

LLM agents are opening a new paradigm for research, in which agents
themselves propose ideas, run experiments, and iterate on tasks that
would take a skilled researcher days [OpenAI (2026)](#bib.bib27); [Wen
et al. (2026)](#bib.bib28). In systems research, AI-Driven Research for
Systems (ADRS) realizes this paradigm through an iterative process in
which LLMs generate candidate designs, evaluate their performance, and
refine them using the resulting feedback [Cheng et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib1). The same process now drives data-center scheduling,
serving policies, load balancing, and database optimization [Novikov et
al. (2025)](#bib.bib17); [Hamadanian et al. (2026)](#bib.bib18); [Lange
et al. (2026)](#bib.bib19); [Cheng et al. (2026)](#bib.bib2). As LLMs
take on more of these steps, they must also interpret evaluation results
and decide which candidate designs to retain or revise.

![Refer to caption](2611.10329v1/figure-1-symbolic.png)

Figure 1: Simulator-assisted evaluation in ADRS. A modeling limitation
can invalidate its recommendation.

Simulators support these evaluations with a software model of a computer
system that predicts how a candidate design performs under a given
workload. This makes evaluation tractable without deploying candidates
on real hardware [Agrawal et al. (2024a)](#bib.bib9); [Cheng et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib1); [Cheng et al. (2026)](#bib.bib2). To remain
scalable, simulators model system behavior at a chosen level of
detail [Heidemann et al. (2001a)](#bib.bib16).

The details that simulators approximate or omit introduce modeling
limitations. For example, ignoring competition for shared network
bandwidth lets a simulator scale to thousands of accelerators but can
underestimate transfer delays [Won et al. (2023)](#bib.bib13). Such a
limitation may alter predicted performance while leaving the best
candidate unchanged, or it may change which candidate to select for a
particular workload [Song et al. (2015)](#bib.bib15). Using a simulator
well therefore requires judging the decision impact of its limitations,
that is, whether they matter for the decision at hand [Heidemann et al.
(2001b)](#bib.bib11). As LLMs take over these decisions, they must make
this judgment themselves, yet how well they do so remains understudied.

[Figure 1](#S1.F1 "In 1 Introduction ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")
illustrates such a case, in which a cost that the limitation adds
reverses the ranking of two designs and thereby invalidates the
simulator’s recommendation. We argue that this judgment is the form of
systems understanding that ADRS relies on: an LLM need not predict a
system’s performance on its own, but it must recognize when a simulator
of that system can be trusted for a decision. Existing evaluations do
not isolate this judgment: whether a simulator’s modeling limitations
invalidate its recommendation for a given design decision. We therefore
ask three questions:

- •
  RQ1: How does simulator evidence shape the design decisions of LLMs?
- •
  RQ2: Can LLMs judge the decision impact of a simulator’s modeling
  limitations?
- •
  RQ3: Can LLMs improve this judgment via their self-correction
  capability?

To answer these questions, we introduce Siris, an LLM evaluation
framework for simulator-assisted system design review. Siris mimics the
modeling limitations of real-world simulators by injecting controlled
perturbations, small code changes to how the simulator represents work,
costs, or resource interactions. For each perturbation, Siris pairs two
workloads on which the perturbed simulator recommends the same design.
The reference simulator supports that recommendation on one workload
(upheld) but favors another design on the other (overturned).

Siris operationalizes judgment as correct design selection across upheld
and overturned problems. It measures judgment by overall accuracy, the
mean of the accuracies on the two problem types. A fixed candidate
preference, or a rule that always follows or always rejects the
presented recommendation, solves at most one problem of each pair.
Disposition summarizes the imbalance between the two accuracies. We
measure judgment and disposition at every level of simulator evidence
and compare them before and after a review turn that elicits
self-correction. Our contributions are as follows:

- •
  We argue for evaluating systems understanding in ADRS through
  judgments of when simulator limitations invalidate a design
  recommendation.
- •
  We propose Siris, which introduces modeling limitations through
  controlled perturbations and measures the judgment and disposition of
  LLMs on paired upheld and overturned problems.
- •
  Evaluating thirteen frontier-level LLMs, we find that most LLMs show
  limited judgment even when they identify the limitation, and that
  inspection instructions and self-correction often shift disposition
  more than they raise judgment.

### 2.1 Simulator-Assisted Systems Research

Simulation-based evaluation. In systems research, a simulator is an
executable model used to estimate how a design performs under a
specified workload. The workload describes the work to process, while
the model represents relevant system components and their interactions.
For example, researchers can compare routing algorithms under the same
network traffic by simulating packet movement and resource contention
and comparing the predicted latency and throughput [Jiang et al.
(2013)](#bib.bib46). This allows candidate designs to be evaluated
without deploying each on the target system.

Simulator use in ADRS. ADRS systems such as AlphaEvolve [Novikov et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib17) and ShinkaEvolve [Lange et al. (2026)](#bib.bib19)
run LLM-driven program search, in which evaluator scores select the
candidates that seed subsequent changes. In simulator-assisted ADRS,
this evaluator is a simulator, so its results determine how each design
is assessed. The same results also guide which designs LLM agents
explore next. Glia [Hamadanian et al. (2026)](#bib.bib18) refines
designs by analyzing simulation experiments, and Database ADRS [Cheng et
al. (2026)](#bib.bib2) goes further by co-evolving a simulator with
candidate policies in its buffer-cache study.

### 2.2 Modeling Limitations and Decisions

Modeling limitations. Simulators keep evaluation tractable by modeling
only the detail that their designers judge relevant to the research
question [Heidemann et al. (2001a)](#bib.bib16).
[Table 1](#S2.T1 "In 2 Background ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")
lists examples of such choices that simulator authors document,
including omitted operations, summarized request state, simplified
surrounding components, and idealized load or communication.

Decision impact. Such choices matter to a design decision only through
their effect on the comparison between candidates. Ranking-and-selection
analyses show that an equal additive error across alternatives cancels
in pairwise differences, whereas candidate-dependent errors can widen,
narrow, or reverse a performance gap [Song et al. (2015)](#bib.bib15),
and architecture studies warn that relative trends may not survive
simulator errors that interact with the evaluated technique [Nowatzki et
al. (2015)](#bib.bib21). Documented examples include errors that distort
performance gaps [Heidemann et al. (2001a)](#bib.bib16) and errors that
reverse design rankings [Lin et al. (2025)](#bib.bib14). Judging
decision impact therefore requires connecting a limitation’s effect on
costs and resource interactions to the specific candidates and workload.

### 2.3 Agents under Unreliable Evidence

Imperfect external evidence. Prior work examines how unreliable evidence
affects LLMs. GARAG [Cho et al. (2024b)](#bib.bib51) searches for
low-level document perturbations that affect retrieval and answer
generation in RAG pipelines. [Zhang et al. (2026)](#bib.bib8) show that
persistent misleading feedback can underperform a matched no-feedback
condition, while [Yang et al. (2026a)](#bib.bib23) show that agents can
recognize a conflict yet still adopt corrupted tool content. Siris
shares this concern with the gap between critique and action, examining
it via controlled perturbations of simulator computations.

Simulation-grounded decisions. MechSim [Yang et al. (2026b)](#bib.bib48)
has agents reason over the mechanisms and assumptions of simplified
candidate simulators and test changes through re-execution, scoring
their policy rankings in aggregate against a more detailed oracle
simulator. [Chen et al. (2026)](#bib.bib49) study how LLMs rank fixed
candidate controllers from simulation results under different
information conditions. Siris isolates whether a particular modeling
limitation invalidates a recommendation, scoring upheld and overturned
problems separately. It pairs workloads that share the candidate
designs, the limitation, the metric, and the simulator’s recommendation,
while the reference supports that recommendation on only one workload.

Appropriate reliance. Appropriate reliance involves following correct
advice and rejecting incorrect advice [Schemmer et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib5). Tools Fail [Sun et al. (2024)](#bib.bib52) treats
outputs with task-irrelevant errors as acceptable and finds that models
often reject them. Siris examines a related distinction between
computational accuracy and recommendation validity, since an upheld
problem contains a limitation that changes predictions while the
reference prefers the recommended design.

## 3 Siris Design

Figure 2: Overview of Siris, from constructing paired problems with a
perturbed simulator to scoring LLM choices.

[Figure 2](#S3.F2 "In 3 Siris Design ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")
summarizes Siris, which tests whether an LLM can tell when a modeling
limitation invalidates a simulator’s recommendation. An LLM selects a
design for a workload from fixed candidates. We construct upheld and
overturned problem pairs, vary the simulator evidence the LLM reads, and
collect an initial choice followed by a review. Comparing both choices
with the reference simulator’s answer yields judgment and disposition,
while a separate annotation records whether each response identifies the
modeling limitation.

### 3.1 Problem Construction

Problem format. Each Siris problem is a multiple-choice question whose
options are candidate designs. The question asks which candidate
achieves the best target metric for a given workload, and its reference
answer is the design the reference simulator predicts best under the
fixed system specification. The context is a set of files the LLM reads
with read-only tools: the problem description, namely the system
specification, candidate code, and workload, plus simulator evidence set
by the evidence condition. Each problem is built on a perturbed
simulator, a copy of the reference simulator with one changed
computation. The LLM selects among the given candidates without writing
a new design or repairing the simulator.

Perturbations. Each perturbation is an explicit program change to a
simulator computation that every candidate relies on, adapted from
classic mutation operators [Jia and Harman (2011)](#bib.bib25);
[Papadakis et al. (2019)](#bib.bib26), that inserts a modeling
limitation, any discrepancy in how the simulator represents work, costs,
or resource interactions. Siris admits a change only if varying the
workload can make the recommendation correct on some workloads and wrong
on others, and if it is reviewable against the specification and the
files the LLM reads.
[Table 3](#A2.T3 "In B.1 Serving Problem Kinds ‣ Appendix B Design-Review Protocol ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")
in the appendix lists the perturbations.

Upheld and overturned pairs. LLM agents separate from the evaluated LLMs
build the problems: a builder proposes workloads, and reviewers check
the evidence, as
[Appendix A](#A1 "Appendix A Protocol and Collection Details ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")
describes. For each proposed workload, Siris runs every candidate under
both simulator versions and records their recommendations and whether
the change alters predictions. A problem is upheld when both versions
recommend the same design and overturned when they differ, and the
perturbed simulator’s recommendation is the presented recommendation.

A perturbation pair joins an upheld and an overturned problem that share
the candidates, perturbation, target metric, and presented
recommendation and differ only in workload, and in both the changed
computation alters predictions.
[Figure 2](#S3.F2 "In 3 Siris Design ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")(a)
depicts one such pair. Such pairs arise because candidates differ in how
strongly the change affects them, while the workload sets how much that
difference matters. This contrast tests whether an LLM distinguishes a
limitation’s presence from its impact on the design choice, since
neither identifying the limitation nor a fixed preference, such as
always following, can solve both problems.

Validation. Independent solvers given only the problem description and
the perturbed simulator’s evidence attempt each problem, and an evidence
audit checks whether these files support the reference answer. Siris
drops each failing problem with its pair partner and fixes every problem
and pair before evaluation. This check does not ensure that the problem
description alone suffices.

### 3.2 Evaluation Protocol

We compare evidence conditions on the same problems to study evidence
use, and initial with reviewed choices to study self-correction.

Evidence conditions. In
[Figure 2](#S3.F2 "In 3 Siris Design ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")(b),
an evidence condition adds simulator evidence beyond the problem
description, from none to all of the simulator source, the measured or
specified cost parameters it evaluates, the modeled system’s
configuration, its predictions, and its execution records. The
no-simulator condition adds none, the perturbed condition adds all of
the perturbed simulator’s evidence, and the reference condition adds all
of the reference simulator’s evidence as a control. All conditions of a
problem are scored against the same reference answer. Each conversation
covers one problem under one condition, so the LLM never sees the pair
partner or label, and in the perturbed condition it sees no reference
results and is not told what changed.

Two-turn review. In both turns, the LLM can read the problem’s files
with read-only tools. The first request asks only for a recommendation
with a short rationale and does not mention modeling limitations or the
review that follows, so the initial choice reflects the LLM’s own
reading of the evidence. The second request then asks the LLM to review
that choice and name the modeling limitation, if any, that it considers
consequential. No new evidence or correctness feedback arrives between
the two turns, although the LLM may open files it skipped in the first
turn.
[Figure 3](#S4.F3 "In 4 Experimental Setup ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")
shows a conversation, and
[Appendix B](#A2 "Appendix B Design-Review Protocol ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")
gives the full protocol.

### 3.3 Metrics

Judgment and disposition. For each model, evidence condition, and turn
$`t`$, let $`U_{t}`$ and $`O_{t}`$ denote accuracy on upheld and
overturned problems. A choice is correct only if it matches the
reference answer, so selecting a third design on an overturned problem
remains incorrect. Siris summarizes judgment by the mean of the two
accuracies and disposition by their imbalance:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       J_{t}=\frac{U_{t}+O_{t}}{2},\qquad D_{t}=\frac{U_{t}-O_{t}}{2}.
       ```                                                              |     | (1) |

In percent, $`J_{t}`$ ranges from 0 to 100 and $`D_{t}`$ from $`-50`$ to
$`50`$. Positive $`D_{t}`$ indicates higher upheld accuracy and negative
$`D_{t}`$ the reverse, as in
[Figure 2](#S3.F2 "In 3 Siris Design ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")(c).
This imbalance differs from the rate of following the recommendation,
since an override may select an incorrect alternative. Errors that keep
an invalid recommendation, abandon a valid one, or select a third design
are counted separately.

Review and identification. Review changes are summarized by
$`\Delta J=J_{\mathrm{final}}-J_{\mathrm{initial}}`$ and
$`\Delta D=D_{\mathrm{final}}-D_{\mathrm{initial}}`$, together with
counts of corrected and newly incorrect choices. Every assigned problem
is scored, and a missing or invalid choice is incorrect. Separately,
limitation identification records whether a response identifies the
modeling limitation that the problem’s perturbation introduces, such as
transfers modeled without sharing a GPU’s network interface. A separate
LLM annotates each perturbed response with a fixed rubric, blind to
labels, reference answers, and model identity, and identification earns
no credit for the design choice, as
[Section B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Scoring and Analysis ‣ Appendix B Design-Review Protocol ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")
details.

Judgment and disposition under the perturbed simulator, unreachable
regions shaded.

Simulator and candidate designs. We instantiate Siris for LLM serving
with a simulator based on LLMServingSim [Cho et al.
(2024a)](#bib.bib12)¹¹ 1
[https://github.com/casys-kaist/LLMServingSim](https://github.com/casys-kaist/LLMServingSim),
whose unperturbed version serves as the reference. The simulator’s cost
parameters are per-step costs measured on GPUs and interpolated over
token counts, and its configuration fixes the GPUs, model, replicas, and
KV cache memory. The four candidates, shown under neutral labels, port
designs from recent serving systems for three design problems: request
routing [Zheng et al. (2024)](#bib.bib35); [Srivatsa et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib36); [Yuan et al. (2026)](#bib.bib37), prefill-to-decode
handoff [Zhong et al. (2024)](#bib.bib38); [Patel et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib39), and local scheduling with chunked prefill [Agrawal
et al. (2024b)](#bib.bib40). Routing and handoff score p95 end-to-end
latency, and local scheduling scores p95 time to first token.
[Section B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Serving Problem Kinds ‣ Appendix B Design-Review Protocol ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")
gives details.

Perturbations and evaluation set. We inject seven perturbations that
omit, simplify, or miscompute parts of the simulated work, costs, or
resource interactions in these design problems, such as limiting
prefix-reuse credit, as controlled changes for this study rather than
reported defects of LLMServingSim. Construction and validation yield 58
problems in 29 perturbation pairs, and
[Table 2](#A1.T2 "In A.1 Construction and Coverage ‣ Appendix A Protocol and Collection Details ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")
in the appendix breaks them down by problem kind.

Models and repetitions. We evaluate thirteen GPT, Grok, and Gemini LLMs
as agents with high reasoning effort, repeating each problem three times
per condition and pooling the repetitions.

Condition coverage. All thirteen models run every problem in the
no-simulator, perturbed, and reference conditions, and GPT-6.1 Sol and
GPT-5.6 Sol also run three evidence-component conditions. These keep the
perturbed simulator’s code, cost parameters, and configuration and add
neither, only the execution records, or only the predictions.

## 5 Results

### 5.1 Simulator Evidence

Judgment by condition.
[Figure 4](#S4.F4 "In 4 Experimental Setup ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")(a)
reports each model’s judgment on its final choices under each evidence
condition. As a baseline, the follow rule always selects the presented
recommendation. It solves every upheld problem and no overturned
problem, scoring $`J=50`$ and $`D=+50`$ under the perturbed simulator.
Without simulator evidence, every model scores near chance, and with the
reference simulator, all but Grok 4.7 reach near-perfect judgment.
Neither condition thus reveals how well a model judges simulator
evidence.

Perturbed simulator. The perturbed bars in
[Figure 4](#S4.F4 "In 4 Experimental Setup ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")(a)
show that every model’s judgment rises above its no-simulator level.
This improvement tends to grow with model recency within each family.
GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol approach their reference-simulator judgment,
whereas the other models stay closer to the follow rule. Perturbed
simulator evidence thus remains useful, and judgment under it separates
models that accuracy without a simulator or with a sound one cannot
distinguish, making it more informative for ADRS.
[Table 5](#A2.T5 "In B.1 Serving Problem Kinds ‣ Appendix B Design-Review Protocol ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")
in the appendix gives exact values.

Distinct decision profiles.
[Figure 4](#S4.F4 "In 4 Experimental Setup ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")(b)
places each model’s final choices under the perturbed simulator by
judgment and disposition. Judgment grows to the right, and positive
disposition means higher accuracy on upheld than on overturned problems.
GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol occupy the region with high judgment and
similar upheld and overturned accuracies. Models with similar judgment
can nevertheless differ substantially in disposition. GPT-6 Sol and Grok
4.7, for example, score 66 and 67 in judgment but $`+29`$ and $`+10`$ in
disposition. The two panels together thus show that perturbed simulator
evidence distinguishes the models in both overall accuracy and decision
behavior.

Evidence components. We next vary the evidence components for GPT-5.6
Sol and GPT-6.1 Sol, which have distinct dispositions in
[Figure 4](#S4.F4 "In 4 Experimental Setup ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")(b).
Each model receives the simulator code, cost parameters, and
configuration, either alone or with one of the simulator’s outputs, the
execution records or the predictions.
[Figure 5](#S5.F5 "In 5.1 Simulator Evidence ‣ 5 Results ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?"),
which labels this bundle Code, shows that Code alone yields judgment
close to or above that with the full perturbed evidence, although the
simulator code contains the perturbation. Adding either output lowers
judgment in both models, but their effects on disposition differ.
Execution records raise disposition in both models, whereas predictions
raise it for GPT-5.6 Sol and lower it for GPT-6.1 Sol. For these two
models, most of the gain from simulator evidence is thus available
without its outputs, and the outputs shift the balance between problem
types without consistently improving judgment.
[Table 6](#A2.T6 "In B.1 Serving Problem Kinds ‣ Appendix B Design-Review Protocol ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")
in the appendix gives exact values for both models.

Figure 5: Judgment and disposition by the simulator evidence available.
Code denotes the simulator code, cost parameters, and configuration.

### 5.2 Decision Impact

Paired decisions.
[Figure 4](#S4.F4 "In 4 Experimental Setup ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")(b)
separates models that perform well on both problem types from those
whose correct choices concentrate on upheld problems. Solving both
problems of a perturbation pair requires keeping the presented
recommendation on one workload and replacing it on the other, even
though both problems contain the same limitation.
[Table 9](#A2.T9 "In B.2 Result Counts ‣ Appendix B Design-Review Protocol ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")
in the appendix shows that GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol solve both
problems in 79 and 65 of 87 pair attempts, 29 pairs in three
repetitions, whereas every other model solves fewer than half. We next
relate these choices to limitation identification.

Figure 6: Decisions among responses that identify the limitation. End
labels count identifying responses.

Decisions after identification.
[Figure 6](#S5.F6 "In 5.2 Decision Impact ‣ 5 Results ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")
shows that about a quarter of the responses that identify the limitation
still select a design other than the reference answer, and every model
makes such errors. Even GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, which identify it
in nearly every response, still abandon some valid recommendations, on
upheld problems where the limitation changes predicted values but leaves
the reference answer unchanged. These errors increase p95 latency under
the reference simulator by a median of 14% per problem for the eight
models with loss measurements, as
[Section B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Result Counts ‣ Appendix B Design-Review Protocol ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")
details. Identifying the limitation therefore does not ensure a correct
decision, and evaluating identification alone would miss these errors.
[Table 10](#A2.T10 "In B.2 Result Counts ‣ Appendix B Design-Review Protocol ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")
in the appendix gives the exact counts for each error type.

Figure 7: Perturbed-simulator results with the standard and
instructed-inspection prompts. Identifying is the share of responses
that identify the limitation.

Instructed inspection. The share of conversations that read the
simulator code changed by the perturbation ranges from 13% to 100%
across models, with similar shares under both simulators. Several models
read it mostly during the review. GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-5.6 Luna, for
example, read it in 80% and 72% of conversations but in only 4% and 2%
of first turns.
[Table 7](#A2.T7 "In B.1 Serving Problem Kinds ‣ Appendix B Design-Review Protocol ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")
in the appendix gives the rates per model, turn, and simulator.

[Figure 7](#S5.F7 "In 5.2 Decision Impact ‣ 5 Results ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")
therefore compares GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-5.6 Sol, and GPT-5.6 Luna under the
perturbed simulator with and without an instruction to read this code
and check it against the system specification before recommending. The
instruction substantially increases limitation identification in GPT-5.6
Sol and GPT-5.6 Luna, but does not consistently improve their judgment.
Their disposition changes more than their judgment, while GPT-6.1 Sol,
which already inspects this code, changes little. Because the
instruction also suggests a mismatch between the simulator and the
specification, this comparison does not isolate the effect of
inspection. Increased limitation identification thus does not reliably
improve decisions on whether a recommendation should stand.
[Table 8](#A2.T8 "In B.1 Serving Problem Kinds ‣ Appendix B Design-Review Protocol ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")
in the appendix gives exact counts for all three models.

### 5.3 Self-Correction

Figure 8: Change from initial (hollow) to final (filled) choices through
the review turn.

Review trajectories.
[Figure 8](#S5.F8 "In 5.3 Self-Correction ‣ 5 Results ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")
connects each model’s initial choices under the perturbed simulator to
the final choices in
[Figure 4](#S4.F4 "In 4 Experimental Setup ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")(b),
so each arrow’s horizontal and vertical extents give the review’s
$`\Delta J`$ and $`\Delta D`$. GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol begin with
high overturned accuracy and improve mainly by restoring valid
recommendations abandoned in the first turn. Several other models
correct invalid recommendations they initially kept, while three remain
near the follow rule. Overall, twelve of the thirteen models move toward
more similar upheld and overturned accuracies.

Corrections and new errors. These movements yield different gains in
judgment.
[Table 4](#A2.T4 "In B.1 Serving Problem Kinds ‣ Appendix B Design-Review Protocol ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")
in the appendix shows that review corrects 31 choices and introduces 10
new errors for GPT-5.6 Sol, raising $`J`$ by 12 points. For GPT-5.6
Terra, 17 corrections are offset by 15 new errors, yielding only a
1-point gain despite a large change in disposition. Review thus tends to
reduce the imbalance between problem types, while its gains in judgment
vary across models and can be offset by new errors.

## 6 Discussion

Broadening the problem space. While our case study focuses on LLM
serving, Siris can extend to other system domains whose simulators
likewise trade fidelity for speed and scale in ways that can change
design decisions, as
[Table 1](#S2.T1 "In 2 Background ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")
shows. Doing so requires a reference that identifies the best design per
workload, workloads on which a perturbation yields both upheld and
overturned problems, and inspectable evidence. Documented limitations of
existing simulators could further supply naturally occurring problems
when a reference establishes their decision impact. Future work could
also inject several limitations at once, whose effects may compound or
cancel out, and define decision impact by their combined effect. It
could likewise move beyond multiple-choice selection of the best design
to other question formats, such as ranking all candidates or proposing a
revised design, defining decision impact for each format.

Integrating Siris into ADRS. Beyond design review task, Siris can be
extended to iterative ADRS workflows to study how judgments shape later
proposals and final designs. In workflows that select candidates
directly by evaluator scores, such as AlphaEvolve [Novikov et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib17), search pressure may favor designs that exploit
simulator limitations, so an extension could test whether an explicit
LLM review results improves the search. In workflows where LLMs already
interpret simulation results, such as Glia [Hamadanian et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib18), the evaluation could track whether they retain or
override the simulator’s recommendation across iterations. When LLMs
also modify the simulator, as in Database ADRS [Cheng et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib2), the evaluation would need to record the designs and
evidence at each iteration, and to keep a reference independent of the
evolving simulator. This would connect judgment on individual decisions
to the designs that ADRS ultimately produces.

Choosing additional evidence. Siris could also evaluate whether LLMs
decide what to measure before selecting a design. When the presented
evidence leaves a comparison unresolved, an LLM could request a targeted
measurement under a budget, testing whether it recognizes the
uncertainty and gathers information that resolves it. Since more
evidence does not uniformly improve decisions in our study, scoring
should weigh the final design against the cost of the measurements.

## 7 Related Work

Simulator validation. Simulation validation assesses fidelity relative
to intended use [Heidemann et al. (2001b)](#bib.bib11), and
Proteus [Duan et al. (2024)](#bib.bib10) also checks whether its
predictions preserve the ordering of parallelization strategies.
Simthesizer [Kim et al. (2026)](#bib.bib20) has a coding agent extend a
serving simulator from feature requests and validates extensions by
throughput error. Decision-focused learning evaluates predictions by the
quality of decisions they induce [Wilder et al. (2019)](#bib.bib6);
[Elmachtoub and Grigas (2022)](#bib.bib7), and Siris evaluates whether
agents judge this decision impact when reading a simulator with a
modeling limitation.

Research agents and review. Research-agent benchmarks such as
MLE-bench [Chan et al. (2025)](#bib.bib32), RE-Bench [Wijk et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib34), and ScienceAgentBench [Chen et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib33) score completed research tasks. MIRAGE [Fu et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib4) varies guidance fidelity and contextual relevance,
while [Xie et al. (2024)](#bib.bib31) study conflicts between external
evidence and parametric knowledge. [Huang et al. (2024)](#bib.bib29)
find that intrinsic self-correction often fails on reasoning tasks, and
[Kamoi et al. (2024)](#bib.bib30) conclude that it helps mainly when
reliable external feedback exists. In code review, prompts asking for
explanations and fixes can increase rejection of correct
implementations [Jin and Chen (2026)](#bib.bib50). Siris scores one
design decision under controlled simulator evidence and records the
corrections and new errors of a review turn without added feedback.

## 8 Conclusion

Siris evaluates whether LLMs judge the decision impact of simulator
modeling limitations, using workload pairs on which the same limitation
upholds or overturns the presented recommendation. Across thirteen LLMs,
perturbed simulator evidence reveals differences in design decisions
that accurate recommendations largely obscure. Identifying a limitation
does not ensure a correct choice. Inspection instructions and
self-correction often shift disposition more than they raise judgment.
Evaluating LLMs for ADRS therefore requires scoring the decisions that
follow limitation identification, counting both error directions
together. We plan to publicly release the Siris artifact.

## Limitations

Measured construct. Siris measures systems understanding through design
choices under controlled simulator limitations. High accuracy shows
successful decisions on these problems but does not establish which
reasoning produced each choice or how it transfers to a complete ADRS
workflow.

Reference-defined answers. Correct choices are defined by the reference
simulator under a fixed system specification, and the reference is not a
perfect model of the real system. Upheld and overturned labels concern
the top-1 design, while smaller margins and lower-rank changes can also
matter to a design decision. Selection loss likewise measures a gap
within the reference simulator.

Real-system outcomes. A choice that matches the reference answer is
correct for a particular specification and simulator, and its advantage
on real hardware is untested. The real-system illustration in
[Appendix C](#A3 "Appendix C Real-System Illustration ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")
covers particular policies, one workload trace, two A100 GPUs, and two
launches. Its p95 TTFT winner is a policy that both simulator versions
recommend, and its throughput winner is unresolved, so it shows that a
simulator comparison can connect to measured performance and contains no
case in which an LLM improves real performance by overturning an invalid
recommendation.

Problem space and exposure. The study covers one domain, LLM serving,
one simulator family, and one perturbation per problem. The 29 pairs
cover three design problems and seven perturbations selected for review,
and each change form appears in one design problem, so the study cannot
separate the effect of the problem from that of the perturbation. All
problems were constructed and inspected during development, and
repetitions vary responses on the same problems without adding new
situations. The results compare the tested models on these problems and
do not establish a general model ranking or deployment performance.

Evidence components. The evidence-component study covers two models and
provides the simulator code, cost parameters, and configuration
together. It therefore characterizes this evidence bundle and the effect
of adding simulator outputs, without separating the contribution of the
code from that of the numerical system information.

Identification annotation. Limitation identification is annotated from
public responses by LLM annotators that agree closely, which shows
reproducible labels but cannot remove biases they share. A stated
limitation records what the LLM wrote, and the review asks only for
consequential limitations, so neither statement nor omission reveals the
computation behind a choice.

Self-correction through review. We call changes between the two turns
self-correction, but a single review turn is our only probe of it, so
the results describe the effect of this turn on design choices. Besides
the same evidence packet, the review lets the LLM open files it skipped
and directs attention to the simulator and its modeling limitations. Its
corrections and new errors therefore combine reconsideration with extra
computation, newly read files, and prompt-induced doubt. Separating
these factors requires a continuation with the same extra computation or
an independent second attempt, which we did not run, so the results do
not show how well these models self-correct in general or whether review
outperforms other uses of extra inference [Kamoi et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib30).

Inference settings. Reasoning effort is the requested setting, which
does not imply equal computation across providers.

### A.1 Construction and Coverage

| Reuse granularity  | 6     | 12       | 468           | 1,404 |

Table 2: Evaluation set by problem kind. Each pair has one upheld and
one overturned problem, and conversations count those assigned to
thirteen models with three repetitions in each of the three evidence
conditions.

Perturbation scope. Each perturbation realizes an abstraction error or
an incorrect implementation of a specified computation, two sources of
simulation error [Gutierrez et al. (2014)](#bib.bib22) that a reader can
detect by comparing the simulator source with the specification. The
evaluated changes therefore form a selected sample of simulator errors,
and uncertainty in the specification, data validity [Sargent
(2013)](#bib.bib24), and interacting limitations lie outside this
evaluation.

Admission criteria. The current evaluation set admits a problem when its
execution is valid and repeatable, both simulator versions have a unique
winner, the changed computation executes and alters predicted values in
upheld problems, and the presented evidence supports the reference
answer.
[Section B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Presented Evidence and Validation ‣ Appendix B Design-Review Protocol ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")
describes the evidence-validation procedure and its exclusions.

Adaptive proposals. An LLM Builder proposes policies and trace
generators within fixed construction criteria and revises proposals
using simulator feedback. Every executed proposal freezes its code,
exact input, sources, and measurement contract. An independent Critic
and Arbiter review the evidence, while automatic failures remain
binding. If confirmation informed a revision, the changed proposal
requires fresh confirmation.

Construction roles. The discovery and confirmation traces define
simulator-construction roles independently of agent-evaluation splits.
Development exposure, earlier failed proposals, and exact-trace-only
qualification retain their original status. Metrics sharing a simulator
execution do not multiply independent workload samples.

### A.2 Data Composition

Reuse of earlier material. Candidates, workloads, and simulator
executions from an earlier problem bank, which contains only overturned
problems, enter the evaluation only under the same eligibility, pairing,
and public-evidence criteria as new material. These criteria include the
packet validation in
[Section B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Presented Evidence and Validation ‣ Appendix B Design-Review Protocol ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?"),
and the evaluation set was fixed before the evaluated agents responded.
The construction records document reused items, exclusion reasons, and
development exposure.

### A.3 Real-System Case Protocol

Policies and input. The illustrative measurement uses 144 requests,
arriving eight at a time every 0.12 seconds. Input lengths are 64, 256,
768, and 1,536 tokens, and output lengths are 16, 64, and 96 tokens,
with 12 requests per length combination. All four policies process the
same trace, with 32 total measured executions across two launches.
Warm-up and environment checks are excluded from the reported metrics.

Uncertainty procedure. The recorded procedure jointly resamples policy
vectors within each launch using 20,000 bootstrap draws. For each
metric, it constructs simultaneous 95% intervals over the six policy
pairs. A resolved winner must beat all three alternatives under these
intervals, rank uniquely first in at least seven of eight repetitions,
and lead within each launch and overall. The intervals are conditional
on the observed launches and have limited tail-probability support from
four repetitions per launch.

### A.4 Evidence Replay

Replay checks. The replay protocol reconstructs question assembly,
retrieval, response scoring, and aggregation from fixed evidence.
Negative checks test mismatched sources, labels, instructions, and
public-evidence boundaries. Fresh-environment checks compare the
resulting questions, field scores, and analysis denominators with their
stored references.

Reuse contract. The protocol fixes problem identity, condition matching,
activation and recommendation checks, and the connection from presented
evidence to choices. A different environment must supply policy,
workload, metric, and simulator semantics together with inspectable
evidence. Evaluating another agent on fixed evidence can reuse the same
simulator records. The serving implementation supplies these bindings
for scheduling policies and simulator costs.

## Appendix B Design-Review Protocol

### B.1 Serving Problem Kinds

|                                                                                                              |                                                                               |                        |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| Problem kind                                                                                                 | Perturbed computation                                                         | Change form            |
| Request routing: which replica serves each request, among load-only, SGLang-inspired, Preble, and DualMap    |                                                                               |                        |
| Prefix cap                                                                                                   | Prefix reuse is credited only up to 512 tokens                                | Value or constant      |
| Reuse granularity                                                                                            | Prefix reuse is credited only in 256-token units                              | Value or constant      |
| Prefill-to-decode handoff: where decode runs after prefill, among stay on source and three remote placements |                                                                               |                        |
| Shared NIC                                                                                                   | Transfers use a dedicated link per GPU pair instead of a shared NIC           | Omission               |
| Local scheduling: the prefill chunk cap per step, among 16, 24, and 32 tokens and no cap                     |                                                                               |                        |
| Query interpolation                                                                                          | Step-cost lookup omits interpolation along the query axis                     | Omission               |
| Step aggregation                                                                                             | Step cost comes from the largest request instead of the sum                   | Aggregation            |
| Coordinate swap                                                                                              | Step-cost lookup swaps the query and KV coordinates                           | Variable or coordinate |
| Interpolation arithmetic                                                                                     | Interpolation computes $`y_{0}+r\,y_{1}`$ instead of $`y_{0}+r(y_{1}-y_{0})`$ | Arithmetic or sign     |

Table 3: Design problems and problem kinds in the serving instantiation.
Each design problem compares four designs, and each problem kind
perturbs one simulator computation that all four rely on.

Change forms. The seven perturbations cover five forms adapted from
mutation operators: replacing a value, omitting a cost or contention
term, changing how costs aggregate, swapping lookup coordinates, and
altering interpolation arithmetic. They are controlled changes for this
study rather than reported defects of LLMServingSim.

Routing. Load-only, SGLang-inspired, Preble, and DualMap send the same
requests to different replicas, so the same prefix-accounting change
produces different executions and costs for each. Workloads vary shared
prefixes and load.

Handoff and local scheduling. Handoff compares staying on the prefill
source with three remote decode placements, and document length sets the
size of the state each transfer moves. Local scheduling compares prefill
chunk caps of 16, 24, 32, and full, and output length changes concurrent
decode and therefore which cost lookups the perturbation affects.

### B.3 Presented Evidence and Validation

Conversation protocol. In the perturbed and reference conditions, the
file list covers the system specification, candidate code, workload,
simulator source, cost parameters, configuration, per-design
predictions, and per-design execution records. The no-simulator
condition lists only the specification, candidate code, and workload,
and its review omits the follow-or-reconsider and limitation fields.
Each turn may list, read, and search these files, and no tool executes
or modifies code. Neither turn names the limitation, its location, or
the number of limitations, and the review supplies no new information,
although the LLM may then read files it did not open in the first turn.

| Provided to the agent                                    | Held by the evaluator                          |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| System specification                                     | Perturbation type and location                 |
| Candidate code, workload, target metric                  | Reference implementation and source difference |
| Presented simulator code, cost parameters, configuration | Reference execution, metrics, and winner       |
| Presented predictions and execution records              | Pair partner’s packet and reference answer     |
| Read-only search and reading tools                       | Upheld or overturned label and pair membership |

Table 12: Information boundary of the design review.

System specification. The specification defines placement, topology,
cache-reuse semantics, and the axes, units, and interpolation of the
cost parameters for each environment. It may help an agent notice a
limitation, but it states no location, fix, or reference answer. Each
specification is fixed before collection.

Packet validation. Two blind solvers attempted each candidate problem
with only the presented packet, and an evidence audit checks that this
evidence supports the reference answer, using the reference execution
only to confirm consistency. Five routing candidates are excluded,
either because the presented evidence cannot order the two leading
designs or because the leaders fall within 1 ms of each other when
recomputed from it.

Concealment. Answer files, the reference source, and the reference
execution lie outside every tool’s accessible scope. We check prompts,
returned passages, filenames, summaries, comments, and tests for target
values and implementation-history cues. All receipts match the frozen
manifest of evidence trees and prompts.

### B.4 Scoring and Analysis

Choices. A problem is solved when the final choice equals the reference
answer, and pair accuracy, which the appendix tables report, requires
correct final choices on both problems of a pair under the same model,
condition, and repetition, the two-instance form of contrast
consistency [Gardner et al. (2020)](#bib.bib47). Each problem is a
separate conversation, and initial and final choices are retained
separately. Wrong choices are classified by design identity into
abandoning a correct recommendation, keeping a wrong one, and replacing
a wrong one with a design other than the reference answer.

Rationale annotation. A separate LLM annotator classified each perturbed
response with a fixed rubric, blind to labels, reference answers, and
model identity. The rubric records whether the response identifies the
perturbed limitation, whether it did so in the first turn, whether it
links the limitation to a specific design, and which impact it claims. A
second annotator independently labeled 200 responses and agreed on
identification for 198 ($`\kappa=0.98`$). For the eight models annotated
first, 623 of the 624 responses with a valid choice that do not identify
the limitation keep the presented recommendation, which follows largely
from the review asking for a reason whenever the agent departs. This
annotation describes responses and never enters pair accuracy.

Collection. Each model uses the same read-only tools under the
perturbed, reference, and no-simulator conditions with three
repetitions. The main evaluation comprises 6,786 assigned conversations,
thirteen models over 58 problems, three conditions, and three
repetitions. Conversations without a valid final choice remain in the
assigned denominators as incorrect.

### B.5 Auxiliary Contrasts

Arms and pairs. Each auxiliary batch draws one pair by a fixed seed from
each of five perturbations, the two routing perturbations, handoff,
query interpolation, and step aggregation, and the second batch draws
only pairs unused by the first. The predictions-only condition lists the
specification, candidate code, workload, and per-design predictions, and
its review asks the agent to check the recommendation against these
files. The comparison condition uses the full-evidence packet and
inserts the following sentence before the review’s response format: “If
you judge that a modeling limitation exists, compare whether its effect
is the same for all candidates or differs between them, and whether
there is evidence that overturns a candidate’s existing advantage,
before deciding the final candidate. Do not drop or keep the
recommendation merely because a limitation exists.” Conversation
sessions cannot be forked after the first turn, so the comparison
condition runs as independent conversations with the same first-turn
prompt. Each batch assigns 360 conversations, 120 per condition, and the
auxiliary results are never pooled with the main evaluation. In the
first batch, the guided review restores all nine first-turn departures
from valid recommendations and adds one new departure, whereas the
standard review restores two of seven and adds two. Identifying
responses number 86 under the standard review and 87 under guidance, and
incorrect choices among them fall from 15 to 9, while overturned
problems with the presented design kept number seven and eight. The
overturned problems solved with predictions alone fall almost entirely
in handoff, and in the first batch all seven repeat the same model’s
no-simulator choice.

Representation and replay. Saved-evidence replay reconstructs packets,
independently scores stored responses, and regenerates the reported
analyses in a fresh environment.

## Appendix C Real-System Illustration

Retained measurements. Recorded vLLM [Kwon et al. (2023)](#bib.bib3)
measurements connect the serving comparisons to measured performance.
One retained comparison executes Qwen3-30B-A3B [Yang et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib53) in BF16 on two A100 40GB GPUs and compares arrival
order, short-prefill priority, most-processed priority, and
least-processed priority. The latter three policies use prefill-token
caps of 128, 512, and 256, respectively. Each policy runs eight times on
the same trace, with four matched repetitions in each of two fresh
launches.

Metric-specific outcome. For p95 TTFT, the short-prefill policy has a
mean of 2.24 seconds across the eight run-level measurements and is
uniquely best in all eight repetitions. Its advantage over the nearest
alternative has a simultaneous 95% interval of 6.38 to 6.94 seconds
under the recorded within-metric procedure. Both simulator sources
recommend that policy. For output throughput on the same trace, the
least-processed priority has the highest mean, 735.9 tokens per second,
but its nearest-alternative advantage interval spans $`-3.33`$ to
$`25.69`$ tokens per second, leaving the empirical winner unresolved.

Role in the analysis. These two outcomes show how an inspectable
simulator comparison connects to an actual serving decision with
metric-specific uncertainty. The resolved TTFT result supports that
case, while the throughput result preserves uncertainty even with a
consistent mean ordering.

## Appendix D Case Studies

This appendix examines two perturbation pairs from the evaluation set in
detail. The routing pair compares designs ported from recent serving
systems, and the handoff pair compares decode placements after prefill.
For each pair, we describe the designs, how the perturbation affects
each design’s execution, and three conversations under the perturbed
simulator. The conversations show a model that identifies the limitation
and keeps a valid recommendation, one that identifies it and abandons a
valid recommendation, and one that corrects an invalid recommendation in
the review turn. Excerpts quote tool calls, files, and answers verbatim,
abridged with ellipses and with whitespace in records condensed.
Candidate labels are those shown in each problem, so a design can carry
different labels on the two workloads.

### D.1 Request Routing with Coarse Prefix Credit

| Design          | Behavior                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         | Upheld (s)    | Overturned (s) |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------- | -------------- |
| Load-only       | Sends each request to the replica with the fewest waiting and running requests, then the fewest queued tokens, and never looks at the caches.                                                                                                    | 1.050 / 0.703 | 0.326 / 0.230  |
| SGLang-inspired | Sends each request to the replica whose cache holds the longest prefix of its prompt, breaking ties by the fewest requests and then the fewest tokens.                                                                                           | 1.597 / 1.233 | 0.552 / 0.180  |
| Preble          | Scores each replica by its recent load, the prompt tokens it would prefill, and the cost of evicting cached prefixes weighted by recent use, and when the best reuse covers more than half of the prompt, only replicas with that reuse compete. | 3.445 / 2.737 | 0.763 / 0.660  |
| DualMap         | Hashes the prompt prefix to two candidate replicas and takes the one with more cached reuse if its predicted prefill time meets a 0.6 s TTFT target, otherwise the one with the lower predicted time.                                            | 1.800 / 1.327 | 0.718 / 0.209  |

Table 13: Routing designs and their p95 end-to-end latency under the
perturbed and reference simulators. The cache-aware designs follow
SGLang [Zheng et al. (2024)](#bib.bib35), Preble [Srivatsa et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib36), and DualMap [Yuan et al. (2026)](#bib.bib37). The
reference answer is load-only on the upheld workload and SGLang-inspired
on the overturned one.

Designs and perturbation. Each design decides which of four replicas,
each with its own prefix cache, serves a request, and the target metric
is p95 end-to-end latency.
[Table 13](#A4.T13 "In D.1 Request Routing with Coarse Prefix Credit ‣ Appendix D Case Studies ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")
describes the designs, and load-only is the presented recommendation on
both workloads. When a request is first scheduled, the perturbed
simulator rounds its prefix-cache hit down to a multiple of 256 tokens,
whereas the system specification credits the longest cached prefix in
whole 16-token blocks. The lost credit is recomputed as prefill, and the
perturbation adds these lines to the scheduler:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Workloads. The upheld workload sends 96 measured requests 5 ms apart
over four shared 576-token prefixes with uniform popularity and 20% of
requests on one hot prefix, so load decides the ranking and load-only
stays best by 75% under the reference simulator. The overturned workload
sends 48 measured requests 22 ms apart over eight 928-token prefixes
with Zipf popularity and 40% on one hot prefix, so reuse decides the
ranking and SGLang-inspired is best by 16%. The rounding keeps 512 of
576 creditable tokens of an upheld hit and 768 of 928 of an overturned
hit.

Design-specific impact. The cache-affine designs hit more often and
therefore lose more credit. Over all requests of the overturned
workload, the rounding raises recomputed prompt tokens by 24% for
load-only, 83% for SGLang-inspired and Preble, and 92% for DualMap. The
perturbed simulator therefore overestimates the latency of
SGLang-inspired by 206% and that of DualMap by 244%, against 42% for
load-only, which reverses the ranking. Preble loses as much credit as
SGLang-inspired, but its error is 16%, since its high latency comes from
its placement. On the upheld workload, recomputation also grows faster
for SGLang-inspired than for load-only, by 161% against 56%, but the
load advantage of load-only keeps it first.

Outcomes across models. Of the 39 perturbed conversations per workload,
36 keep the valid upheld recommendation and 15 replace the invalid
overturned one, and 12 repetitions solve both problems. Without
simulator evidence, 10 and 14 are correct.

### D.2 Prefill-to-Decode Handoff with Independent Links

| Design              | Behavior                                                                                                                | Upheld (s)    | Overturned (s) |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------- | -------------- |
| Stay on source      | Decodes on the prefill replica and never moves the KV cache.                                                            | 3.465 / 3.465 | 1.816 / 1.816  |
| Next instance       | Moves the decode to the next replica above the prefill replica.                                                         | 3.771 / 3.771 | 2.424 / 2.424  |
| Least-active remote | Moves the decode to the remote replica with the fewest active calls, not counting transfers still in flight.            | 3.769 / 3.769 | 2.425 / 2.425  |
| Least-outstanding   | Counts active calls plus handoffs sent but not yet arrived, and moves the decode to the remote replica with the fewest. | 2.826 / 3.030 | 1.649 / 2.056  |

Table 14: Handoff designs and their p95 end-to-end latency under the
perturbed and reference simulators. The three remote placements follow
disaggregated serving [Zhong et al. (2024)](#bib.bib38). The reference
answer is least-outstanding on the upheld workload and stay on source on
the overturned one.

Designs and perturbation. Each design decides where the follow-up
requests of a shared document decode after prefill, and the target
metric is p95 end-to-end latency.
[Table 14](#A4.T14 "In D.2 Prefill-to-Decode Handoff with Independent Links ‣ Appendix D Case Studies ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")
describes the designs, and least-outstanding is the presented
recommendation on both workloads. In the modeled system, every KV
transfer leaving a GPU shares its one 10 GbE interface, whereas the
perturbed simulator gives each ordered GPU pair its own link, so
simultaneous transfers from one GPU finish together instead of queuing.
The perturbation replaces the switch topology with per-pair links,
abridged below:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Workloads and design-specific impact. Both workloads send five bursts in
which three follow-ups per prefill replica move their KV caches
together. The overturned workload doubles the shared document and
question to 2,560 and 384 tokens and halves the output to 3 tokens, so
each moved transfer is about twice as large. Only least-outstanding
spreads decodes over seven replicas, so its simultaneous transfers leave
one GPU for different destinations and never queue in the perturbed
simulator. Its mean first-token latency drops from 1.04 to 0.85 s on the
upheld workload and from 1.23 to 0.85 s on the overturned one. Stay on
source sends no transfer, and the other two placements send each burst
to the same few destinations, so their predictions do not change. With
the larger transfers, the corrected latency of least-outstanding rises
past stay on source, which becomes best by 13%, while on the upheld
workload least-outstanding remains best by 14%.

Outcomes across models. Of the 39 perturbed conversations per workload,
37 keep the valid upheld recommendation and 29 replace the invalid
overturned one, and 27 repetitions solve both problems. Without
simulator evidence, 16 and 26 are correct.

shows GPT-6.1 Sol reaching the changed links in its first turn, checking

[Figures 13](#A4.F13 "In D.2 Prefill-to-Decode Handoff with Independent Links ‣ Appendix D Case Studies ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")
and [14](#A4.F14 "Figure 14 ‣ D.2 Prefill-to-Decode Handoff with Independent Links ‣ Appendix D Case Studies ‣ Siris: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation ErrorsMatter in AI-Driven Systems Research?")
show Gemini 3.8 Flash identifying the same limitation on both workloads.
On the overturned workload, it sizes the added transfer delay at about
2.02 s against the reference value of 2.056 s and correctly switches to
stay on source. On the upheld workload, it makes no tool call in the
review and switches to stay on source on a claim of severe contention,
although the reference simulator keeps least-outstanding best by 14%. In
both pairs, the same identification thus leads to opposite decisions,
depending on whether the model sizes the limitation’s effect.
